title: Basic Concepts of Diffraction
short_intro: Diffraction is the bending of light waves around the corners of an obstacle or aperture into the geometrical shadow region. It arises due to the secondary wavelets originating from different points of the same wavefront, as stated by Huygens-Fresnel principle.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of diffraction, distinction between Fresnel and Fraunhofer classes, condition for maxima and minima in single-slit diffraction, and basic wavelength dependence.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Analytical treatment of single-slit intensity distribution, phasor diagram method for resultant amplitude, width of central maximum, angular dispersion, and comparison with interference.

prerequisites: Phase difference and path difference relationships

concept_notes.heading: Wavefront Subdivision and Huygens-Fresnel Principle
bullets: Every point on a propagating wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets.
The resultant optical disturbance at any subsequent point is the superposition of all these secondary wavelets taking their respective phases and amplitudes into account.
Diffraction is fundamentally the interference of a continuous infinity of coherent secondary wavelets originating from the unobstructed portions of a single wavefront.

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Diffraction: Fresnel and Fraunhofer
bullets: Fresnel diffraction occurs when either the source of light, the obstacle/aperture, or the screen (or any combination) is at a finite distance, making the wavefronts incident and emergent spherical or cylindrical.
Fraunhofer diffraction occurs when both the source and the observation screen are effectively at infinite distances from the aperture, achieved experimentally using lenses.
In Fraunhofer diffraction, the incident wavefronts are planar and the diffracted rays forming a particular parallel beam are brought to a focus on the screen.

concept_notes.heading: Distinction Between Interference and Diffraction
bullets: Interference is the superposition of two or more distinct coherent wave trains originating from separate wavefronts (e.g., Young's double slit).
Diffraction is the superposition of continuous secondary wavelets originating from different parts of the same wavefront.

In interference, all bright fringes are generally of equal intensity, whereas in single-slit diffraction, the central maximum is brightest and widest, with subsidiary maxima falling off rapidly in intensity.

concept_notes.heading: Conditions for Maxima and Minima in Single-Slit Diffraction
bullets: Secondary minima occur when the path difference between light rays originating from the top and bottom edges of a slit of width a is an integral multiple of the wavelength lambda.
Principal maxima occur approximately midway between the secondary minima, corresponding to odd multiples of lambda / 2 path difference for consecutive zones.
The central maximum is twice as wide as any of the secondary maxima and contains the vast majority of the incident optical energy.

derivations.title: Fraunhofer Diffraction at a Single Slit
derivations.conditions: Normal incidence of plane wavefront on a slit of width a, observation on a focal plane of a convex lens.
steps: Consider a slit of width a divided into n equal strips. The path difference between rays from the extreme edges of the slit for a diffraction angle theta is given by delta = a sin(theta).
The phase difference between successive strips is beta = (2pi / lambda) (a/n) sin(	heta). Let the total phase difference between the extreme rays be 2alpha = (2pi / lambda) a sin(	heta).
Summing the amplitudes of n secondary wavelets using the polygon method of vector addition yields the resultant amplitude R = A0 (sin(alpha) / alpha), where A0 is the maximum amplitude.
The intensity is proportional to R^2, giving I = I0 (sin(alpha) / alpha)^2.

derivations.title: Position of Secondary Minima in Single-Slit Diffraction
derivations.conditions: Destructive interference conditions across the slit width a.
steps: Divide the slit width a into two equal halves of width a/2. For any ray from the upper half, a corresponding ray from the lower half can be found with a path difference of (lambda / 2).
This mutual cancellation leads to the first minimum when (a/2) sin 	heta = lambda / 2, or a sin 	heta = lambda.
Generalizing this subdivision into 2n equal parts results in destructive interference whenever corresponding destructive pairs cancel out.
Therefore, the condition for the m-th secondary minimum is a sin 	heta = mlambda, where m = pm 1, pm 2, pm 3, ...

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs. Diffraction Parameter (alpha) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A central symmetric peak of height I0 at alpha = 0, flanked by subsidiary secondary maxima of rapidly decreasing heights situated at alpha approx (m + 0.5)pi, with zero intensity at alpha = m*pi.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the rapid attenuation of intensity away from the central axis and highlights that the central maximum has twice the width of subsidiary maxima.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in PGT and TGT exams to test identification of minima positions and relative peak heights.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fresnel's Biprisms or Half-Wave Plate / Zone Plate Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A circular aperture illuminated by a point source, showing concentric circular zones (Fresnel zones) of alternating phase cancellation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how circular obstacles or apertures give rise to Fresnel diffraction patterns like the Poisson spot (Arago spot).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually for differences between Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction geometries.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Single Slit Diffraction Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Monochromatic source, collimating lens L1, slit of width a, diffraction lens L2, and observation screen placed at the focal plane of L2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how infinite distances are simulated in a laboratory bench using lenses for Fraunhofer diffraction observations.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 5000 Å falls normally on a single slit of width 0.2 mm. Calculate the angular position of the first secondary minimum.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: lambda = 5000 Å = 5 x 10^-7 m, a = 0.2 mm = 2 x 10^-4 m, m = 1.
Use the diffraction minimum condition: a sin(theta) = m * lambda.
Substitute values: sin(theta) = (1 * 5 x 10^-7) / (2 x 10^-4) = 2.5 x 10^-3.
Since sin(theta) is very small, theta approx sin(theta) = 2.5 x 10^-3 radians.

solved_numericals.question: A slit of width 0.5 mm is illuminated normally by light of wavelength 589 nm. The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen placed 1.0 m away from the lens. Calculate the linear width of the central maximum.
solution_steps: Identify given data: a = 0.5 mm = 5 x 10^-4 m, lambda = 589 nm = 5.89 x 10^-7 m, f (or D) = 1.0 m.
Recall the formula for linear width of central maximum: beta_0 = 2 * lambda * f / a.
Substitute the values: beta_0 = (2 * 5.89 x 10^-7 * 1.0) / (5 x 10^-4).
Calculate the final numerical value: beta_0 = (11.78 x 10^-7) / (5 x 10^-4) = 2.356 x 10^-3 m.

solved_numericals.question: In a single slit diffraction pattern, the angular width of the central maximum is measured to be 2 degrees when light of wavelength 600 nm is used. Find the width of the slit.
solution_steps: Identify the angular width relation: Total angular width = 2 * theta = 2 * (lambda / a).
Convert angle to radians: 2 degrees = 2 * (pi / 180) rad = (pi / 90) rad. Therefore, half-angle theta = pi / 180 rad.
Use theta = lambda / a to find a: a = lambda / theta.
Substitute lambda = 600 x 10^-9 m and theta = (pi / 180) rad: a = (600 x 10^-9 * 180) / pi.

assumptions_and_limitations: Scalar diffraction theory assumes the light wave can be treated as a scalar wave, ignoring vector polarization effects, which holds well when the aperture dimensions are much larger than the wavelength.
Fraunhofer approximations assume that distances R >> a^2 / lambda, validating the neglect of quadratic phase terms across the aperture.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All bright fringes in a single-slit diffraction pattern have equal intensity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only the central maximum has maximum intensity; subsidiary maxima have drastically lower intensities.
common_misconceptions.why: Unlike interference fringes where amplitudes from two coherent slits remain uniform, diffraction involves varying fractional cancellation across a continuous aperture.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Diffraction only occurs when obstacles are microscopic.
common_misconceptions.correct: Diffraction occurs for obstacles of any size, but it is pronounced only when the obstacle or aperture dimensions are comparable to the wavelength of the wave.
common_misconceptions.why: The diffraction angle theta approx lambda / a is too small to detect easily when aperture a is extremely large compared to lambda.

quick_revision: Diffraction is the bending of waves around edges governed by secondary wavelets from unblocked wavefronts.
Fraunhofer diffraction requires infinite source-screen distances, simulated in labs via lenses.
Minima condition for single slit: a sin(theta) = m*lambda (m != 0).
Central maximum width is twice that of any secondary maximum: beta_0 = 2*lambda*f / a.
